source_batch.unit_label: Module A unit 6 (part 2): Theory of Probability: binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, credit risk, value at risk, option valuation

facts.statement: A random variable X counting successes in n repeated independent trials with success probability p at each trial follows a binomial distribution: f(x) = C(n, x) p^x q^(n-x) for x = 0, 1, ..., n, with q = 1 - p. Mean = np, variance = npq, skewness measure = (1 - 2p)^2 / (npq) and kurtosis measure = 3 + (1 - 6pq) / (npq). The distribution is symmetric if p = q = 0.5, positively skewed if p < 0.5 and negatively skewed if p > 0.5. For the mode let M = (n + 1) p: if M is not an integer the mode is its integral part, and if M is an integer there are two modes, M - 1 and M. Courseware examples: n = 8, p = 1/2 gives P(|X - 4| <= 2) = 119/128; n = 60, p = 0.7 gives mean 42, variance 12.6, standard deviation 3.55 and mode 42.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 120-121, section 6.7 (the courseware states the integer-M rule inconsistently as "M - 2 and M" and "M - 1 and M")

facts.statement: A random variable X taking the values 0, 1, 2, ... is a Poisson random variable with parameter lambda > 0 if f(x) = e^(-lambda) lambda^x / x!, where e is about 2.7183. Examples: misprints on a page, wrong telephone numbers dialled in a day, customers entering a post office in a day. Mean = lambda and variance = lambda; skewness measure = 1/lambda and kurtosis measure = 3 + 1/lambda. The mode is the integral part of lambda if lambda is not an integer, and there are two modes, lambda - 1 and lambda, if it is. Courseware examples: lambda = 1.8 gives P(X = 4) = 0.0723 and P(X >= 2) = 0.538 as printed (0.5372 when recomputed); lambda = 0.5 (accidents per week) gives P(X < 2) = 0.9098, P(X > 2) = 0.0144 and P(no accident in three weeks) = 0.223; for 1.2 misprints a page, ten pages have total mean 12 and P(total = 5) = 0.0127.

The normal distribution has the bell-shaped, symmetric density f(x) = (1 / (sigma sqrt(2 pi))) e^(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)) with parameters mu and sigma squared; the total area is 1, mean = median = mode = mu, the quartile deviation is 0.6745 sigma and the mean deviation 0.7979 sigma. With mu = 0 and sigma squared = 1 the variable is the standard normal Z. A normal variable is standardised by Z = (X - mu) / sigma. Courseware examples: incomes N(800, 400) for 1,000 employees give P(750 < x < 820) = 0.3413 + 0.4938 = 0.8351, P(x > 760) = 0.9772; a battery life N(50, 9) gives P(x > 53) = 0.5 - 0.3413 = 0.1587 and P(53 < x < 55) = 0.4525 - 0.3413 = 0.1112.

Credit risk is the possibility or probability of a loss from a borrower's failure to repay a loan or meet contractual obligations. Three types: credit default risk (loss when the borrower cannot repay in full or when 90 days pass after the due date), concentration risk (arising from significant exposure to one individual, group, company or industry, which can inflict large losses on the core operations of a bank) and country or sovereign risk (a government or central bank unwilling or unable to meet its contractual obligations).

To estimate expected loss in advance a lender uses the exposure at default (EAD, the value of the loan at default), the probability of default (PD) and the loss given default (LGD, the part of the loan that would be lost if default occurs even though some may be recovered). The courseware prints the formula as Expected loss = PD x EAD x (1 - LGD); its Problem 1 (EAD Rs 20,00,000, PD 100 per cent, LGD 50 per cent) gives Rs 10,00,000 and its Problem 2 (EAD Rs 35,00,000, PD 0.20 per cent, LGD 57 per cent) gives Rs 3,010 by that formula. Since the text defines LGD as the part lost, the usual form is Expected loss = PD x LGD x EAD, which gives Rs 3,990 for Problem 2.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 126-127, section 6.10 (the printed formula uses 1 - LGD, which conflicts with the definition of LGD in the same passage)

facts.statement: Value at risk (VaR) is a financial metric that estimates the maximum amount a portfolio could lose over a specified period at a stated level of confidence, such as 95 or 99 per cent. The courseware's formulas are VaR at 95 per cent = [return of the portfolio - 1.65 sigma] x value of the portfolio and VaR at 99 per cent = [return - 2.33 sigma] x value, assuming stock returns are normally distributed with sigma the standard deviation of the returns. Its examples: portfolio Rs 30,000, return 10 per cent and standard deviation 12 per cent, VaR at 95 per cent = (0.10 - 0.198) x 30,000 = -2,940 (9.8 per cent of the portfolio); portfolio Rs 2,50,000, return 15 per cent, standard deviation 10 per cent, VaR at 99 per cent = (0.15 - 0.233) x 2,50,000 = -20,750 (8.3 per cent).
facts.locator: Printed pp. 127-128, section 6.11 (the courseware calls the figures "daily" although its inputs are one-month returns)

facts.statement: An option gives its holder the right, with no obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying asset at a predetermined price on or before a predetermined date; the person who writes the option is obliged to sell or buy if it is exercised. The predetermined price is the strike or exercise price and the date is the maturity date. A European option can be exercised only on the maturity date, an American option on or before it. The price paid for the option is its premium or value.

Factors affecting option price: a higher strike price lowers the call price and raises the put price; a longer time to maturity raises both call and put prices; a higher stock price raises the call price and lowers the put price; a higher risk-free interest rate raises the call price and lowers the put price; higher volatility of the underlying raises both. The value on the date of maturity is the intrinsic value, and before maturity an option also carries time value that falls as maturity approaches.

An option's value cannot be negative. A call is worth at least the stock price minus the present value of the strike price, so C >= max[0, PP - PV(SP)]; a put is worth at least PV(SP) - PP. The binomial option pricing model assumes prices move at discrete intervals, going up by u per cent or down by d per cent at each interval with probability p and 1 - p, over n intervals, so the number of upward moves follows a binomial distribution. The Black-Scholes model assumes prices move continuously and returns are normally distributed: C = N(d1) S - N(d2) K e^(-r(T - t)), with d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)(T - t)] / (sigma sqrt(T - t)) and d2 = d1 - sigma sqrt(T - t), N being the standard normal cumulative distribution; the put follows from put-call parity, P = K e^(-r(T - t)) - S + C. Option traders buy options priced below the model value and sell those priced above it.

payload.title: The binomial distribution
payload.core_explanation_md:
Use the binomial when you count **successes** in a **fixed number n of independent trials**, each with the **same success probability p**. Typical bank cases: the number of loans, out of 20, that go bad, if each does so independently with probability 0.05; the number of cheques, out of 50, returned.

The chance of exactly x successes is the number of ways to place them times the probability of each such sequence: C(n, x) p to the x times q to the (n - x), where q = 1 - p.

Handy summary figures: mean np, variance npq. The **mode** is the whole-number part of (n + 1)p; if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, one below it.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Check the conditions before using it. If trials influence one another, or p changes from trial to trial, the binomial formula will give wrong probabilities.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x}p^x q^{n-x},\quad E(X) = np,\quad V(X) = npq,\quad M = (n+1)p

variables.name: Probability of success in each trial

assumptions: Fixed number of trials.
Each trial has two outcomes, success or failure.
Trials are independent with constant p.
common_errors: Using the binomial when p changes between trials.
Forgetting the combination factor C(n, x).
Reporting only the integral part of M when M is an integer (there are two modes, M - 1 and M).

self_check.prompt_text: n = 10 and p = 0.2. What are the mean, the variance and the mode?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Mean 2, variance 1.6, M = 11 x 0.2 = 2.2 so the mode is 2.

payload.title: Shape of a binomial distribution
payload.core_explanation_md:
The shape follows p:

| p | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| Less than 0.5 | Positively skewed (long right tail): small counts are the most likely |
| Exactly 0.5 | Symmetric |
| More than 0.5 | Negatively skewed (long left tail): large counts are the most likely |

The courseware measures skewness as (1 - 2p) squared over npq, which is zero only when p is 0.5, and kurtosis as 3 + (1 - 6pq)/npq, which moves towards 3 as n grows.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The sign of the skew is read from p. The squared skewness measure given in the courseware cannot itself be negative, so it shows how much asymmetry there is rather than which way.

self_check.prompt_text: Each of 60 loans repays with probability 0.7. Is the distribution of the number repaying skewed to the left or the right?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Negatively skewed (long left tail), because p = 0.7 is above 0.5.

payload.title: The Poisson distribution
payload.core_explanation_md:
The Poisson distribution counts how many times something happens in a **fixed interval** (a day, a page, a week) when the events occur at random at an **average rate lambda** per interval: misprints per page, wrong numbers dialled per day, customers arriving per hour.

The chance of exactly x events is e to the minus lambda times lambda to the x, divided by x factorial.

Two remarkable facts: the **mean and the variance are both lambda**, and for several independent intervals the total is Poisson too, with the rates added (ten pages at 1.2 misprints each give a rate of 12).

The mode is the whole-number part of lambda, or two modes (lambda - 1 and lambda) if lambda is a whole number.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: For "at least" questions use the complement: P(X at least 2) = 1 - P(0) - P(1). Summing infinitely many terms is never needed.

variables.name: Average number of events per interval

assumptions: Events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.
The interval for lambda matches the interval being asked about.
common_errors: Using a weekly rate for a monthly question without rescaling lambda.
Computing "at least" probabilities by adding terms instead of using the complement.
Thinking the variance differs from the mean.

self_check.prompt_text: A branch averages 2.5 failed transactions an hour. What is the rate for a 2-hour period?
self_check.expected_takeaway: lambda = 5, because rates for independent intervals add.

payload.title: Which distribution fits the question?
payload.core_explanation_md:
Three questions pick the model.

| Ask | Binomial | Poisson | Normal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What is counted or measured? | Successes in n trials | Events in an interval | A measurement on a continuous scale |
| Is there a fixed number of trials? | Yes (n) | No upper limit | Not applicable |
| Parameters | n and p | lambda | mu and sigma |
| Mean and variance | np and npq | Both lambda | mu and sigma squared |

Examples: loans out of 20 that default (binomial); wrong numbers dialled in a day (Poisson); daily cash demand in rupees (normal).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The first two give probabilities for exact counts (a mass function). The normal gives probabilities for ranges (areas under a density), and the chance of exactly one value is zero.

self_check.prompt_text: Which model for "the number of customers arriving at a counter in a given hour"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Poisson: events counted in a fixed interval at an average rate.

payload.title: Credit risk and its three faces
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Credit risk** is the chance of a loss because a borrower does not pay as promised. Three types appear in this course:

| Type | What goes wrong | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Credit default risk** | Borrower cannot repay in full, or is 90 days past due | Overdue instalments |
| **Concentration risk** | Too much exposure to one borrower, group or industry | One failure hurts the whole bank |
| **Country (sovereign) risk** | A government or central bank cannot or will not meet its obligations | Lending to a state in distress |

Probability theory enters because default is uncertain: lenders estimate a **probability of default** and use it to price and provision.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Concentration risk is about size, not about whether any one borrower is weak. A large exposure to a healthy borrower is still a concentration.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank lends 40 per cent of its portfolio to one steel group. Which credit risk is this?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Concentration risk: significant exposure to a single group or industry.

payload.title: Value at risk for a normal portfolio
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Value at risk** answers: "over a stated period, with a stated level of confidence, how much could the portfolio lose?" If returns are normal with mean r and standard deviation sigma:

- at **95 per cent** confidence, the worst return is r minus 1.65 sigma;
- at **99 per cent**, it is r minus 2.33 sigma.

Multiply that worst return by the portfolio value. A negative answer is a loss, and VaR is usually quoted as the size of that loss.

The period of the return and of sigma sets the period of the VaR: monthly inputs give a monthly VaR.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The multipliers come from the normal curve: 1.65 leaves about 5 per cent in the lower tail (exactly 1.645) and 2.33 about 1 per cent (exactly 2.326). The method assumes returns really are normal, which is a strong assumption in a crisis.

variables.name: Standard deviation of returns for the period

assumptions: Returns are normally distributed.
r and sigma are for the same period as the VaR.
common_errors: Using the 95 per cent multiplier for a 99 per cent VaR.
Mixing a daily sigma with a monthly return.
Quoting the negative number as a gain.

self_check.prompt_text: Portfolio Rs 2,00,000, mean return 6 per cent, sigma 5 per cent. What is the 95 per cent loss?

payload.title: Options: the words you need
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **option** is a right, not an obligation.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Call** | The right to **buy** the underlying at a fixed price |
| **Put** | The right to **sell** the underlying at a fixed price |
| **Holder** (buyer) | Has the right and pays the premium |
| **Writer** (seller) | Must deliver or buy if the holder exercises |
| **Strike (exercise) price** | The fixed price in the contract |
| **Maturity date** | The last day (or only day) the option can be exercised |
| **European / American** | European: exercise only at maturity. American: any time up to maturity |
| **Premium** | The price of the option |

A forward contract commits both sides; an option lets the holder walk away if the market price is more favourable.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: If the market price beats the strike, a call holder exercises and buys cheaply; if not, the option expires worthless and the holder loses only the premium.

self_check.prompt_text: Who is obliged to act if an option is exercised, the holder or the writer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The writer: the holder has only a right.

payload.title: What moves an option's price
payload.core_explanation_md:
Five factors, and how a **rise** in each affects the price:

| Factor rises | Call price | Put price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strike price | Falls | Rises |
| Time to maturity | Rises | Rises |
| Stock (underlying) price | Rises | Falls |
| Risk-free interest rate | Rises | Falls |
| Volatility | Rises | Rises |

Why volatility helps both: the holder is protected against bad moves (can walk away) but gains from favourable ones, so more uncertainty adds value to either right. Why time helps both: more time means more chance of a favourable move.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Before maturity an option has **time value** on top of its intrinsic value (the difference between stock and strike, if favourable). Time value shrinks to zero at maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: A stock's volatility doubles. What happens to the call and put prices?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both rise, because greater uncertainty makes either right more valuable.

payload.title: Option value bounds and the two pricing models
payload.core_explanation_md:
An option never has negative value, and arbitrage fixes a floor:

- **Call**: worth at least the stock price minus the **present value** of the strike, and never less than zero: max[0, S - PV(K)].
- **Put**: worth at least PV(K) - S (or zero).

Two models give the exact price.

- **Binomial model**: price moves at discrete steps, up or down by set percentages with probabilities p and 1 - p; the number of up moves is binomial.
- **Black-Scholes model**: price moves continuously and returns are normal; the call value uses the standard normal cumulative N(d1) and N(d2) with d1 and d2 built from the stock price, strike, rate, volatility and time.

The put follows from put-call parity: P = K e to the minus r(T - t) minus S plus C.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A trader compares the market price with the model value: buy options priced below it, sell those priced above. The details of the formulas are beyond hand calculation; understand the inputs and the direction of each effect.

formula_spec.latex_expression: C \ge \max[0,\ S - PV(K)],\quad P \ge PV(K) - S,\quad C = N(d_1)S - N(d_2)Ke^{-r(T-t)},\quad P = Ke^{-r(T-t)} - S + C

variables.name: Present value of the strike, K discounted at the risk-free rate
Risk-free rate, volatility and time to expiry

assumptions: Black-Scholes: continuously moving prices and normally distributed returns.
The bounds hold for the stated option style and no arbitrage.
common_errors: Using the strike price instead of its present value in the bound.
Forgetting the floor at zero.
Using N(d2) in place of N(-d2) when writing the put directly (use put-call parity).

items.title: The binomial distribution
items.core_explanation_md:
Use the binomial when you count **successes** in a **fixed number n of independent trials**, each with the **same success probability p**. Typical bank cases: the number of loans, out of 20, that go bad, if each does so independently with probability 0.05; the number of cheques, out of 50, returned.

The chance of exactly x successes is the number of ways to place them times the probability of each such sequence: C(n, x) p to the x times q to the (n - x), where q = 1 - p.

Handy summary figures: mean np, variance npq. The **mode** is the whole-number part of (n + 1)p; if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, one below it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Check the conditions before using it. If trials influence one another, or p changes from trial to trial, the binomial formula will give wrong probabilities.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x}p^x q^{n-x},\quad E(X) = np,\quad V(X) = npq,\quad M = (n+1)p

variables.name: Probability of success in each trial

assumptions: Fixed number of trials.
Each trial has two outcomes, success or failure.
Trials are independent with constant p.
common_errors: Using the binomial when p changes between trials.
Forgetting the combination factor C(n, x).
Reporting only the integral part of M when M is an integer (there are two modes, M - 1 and M).

self_check.prompt_text: n = 10 and p = 0.2. What are the mean, the variance and the mode?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Mean 2, variance 1.6, M = 11 x 0.2 = 2.2 so the mode is 2.

items.title: Shape of a binomial distribution
items.core_explanation_md:
The shape follows p:

| p | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| Less than 0.5 | Positively skewed (long right tail): small counts are the most likely |
| Exactly 0.5 | Symmetric |
| More than 0.5 | Negatively skewed (long left tail): large counts are the most likely |

The courseware measures skewness as (1 - 2p) squared over npq, which is zero only when p is 0.5, and kurtosis as 3 + (1 - 6pq)/npq, which moves towards 3 as n grows.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The sign of the skew is read from p. The squared skewness measure given in the courseware cannot itself be negative, so it shows how much asymmetry there is rather than which way.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Negatively skewed (long left tail), because p = 0.7 is above 0.5.

items.title: The Poisson distribution
items.core_explanation_md:
The Poisson distribution counts how many times something happens in a **fixed interval** (a day, a page, a week) when the events occur at random at an **average rate lambda** per interval: misprints per page, wrong numbers dialled per day, customers arriving per hour.

The chance of exactly x events is e to the minus lambda times lambda to the x, divided by x factorial.

Two remarkable facts: the **mean and the variance are both lambda**, and for several independent intervals the total is Poisson too, with the rates added (ten pages at 1.2 misprints each give a rate of 12).

The mode is the whole-number part of lambda, or two modes (lambda - 1 and lambda) if lambda is a whole number.
items.expanded_explanation_md: For "at least" questions use the complement: P(X at least 2) = 1 - P(0) - P(1). Summing infinitely many terms is never needed.

variables.name: Average number of events per interval

assumptions: Events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.
The interval for lambda matches the interval being asked about.
common_errors: Using a weekly rate for a monthly question without rescaling lambda.
Computing "at least" probabilities by adding terms instead of using the complement.
Thinking the variance differs from the mean.

self_check.prompt_text: A branch averages 2.5 failed transactions an hour. What is the rate for a 2-hour period?
self_check.expected_takeaway: lambda = 5, because rates for independent intervals add.

items.title: Credit risk and its three faces
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credit risk** is the chance of a loss because a borrower does not pay as promised. Three types appear in this course:

| Type | What goes wrong | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Credit default risk** | Borrower cannot repay in full, or is 90 days past due | Overdue instalments |
| **Concentration risk** | Too much exposure to one borrower, group or industry | One failure hurts the whole bank |
| **Country (sovereign) risk** | A government or central bank cannot or will not meet its obligations | Lending to a state in distress |

Probability theory enters because default is uncertain: lenders estimate a **probability of default** and use it to price and provision.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Concentration risk is about size, not about whether any one borrower is weak. A large exposure to a healthy borrower is still a concentration.

items.title: Value at risk for a normal portfolio
items.core_explanation_md:
**Value at risk** answers: "over a stated period, with a stated level of confidence, how much could the portfolio lose?" If returns are normal with mean r and standard deviation sigma:

- at **95 per cent** confidence, the worst return is r minus 1.65 sigma;
- at **99 per cent**, it is r minus 2.33 sigma.

Multiply that worst return by the portfolio value. A negative answer is a loss, and VaR is usually quoted as the size of that loss.

The period of the return and of sigma sets the period of the VaR: monthly inputs give a monthly VaR.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The multipliers come from the normal curve: 1.65 leaves about 5 per cent in the lower tail (exactly 1.645) and 2.33 about 1 per cent (exactly 2.326). The method assumes returns really are normal, which is a strong assumption in a crisis.

assumptions: Returns are normally distributed.
r and sigma are for the same period as the VaR.
common_errors: Using the 95 per cent multiplier for a 99 per cent VaR.
Mixing a daily sigma with a monthly return.
Quoting the negative number as a gain.

items.title: Options: the words you need
items.core_explanation_md:
An **option** is a right, not an obligation.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Call** | The right to **buy** the underlying at a fixed price |
| **Put** | The right to **sell** the underlying at a fixed price |
| **Holder** (buyer) | Has the right and pays the premium |
| **Writer** (seller) | Must deliver or buy if the holder exercises |
| **Strike (exercise) price** | The fixed price in the contract |
| **Maturity date** | The last day (or only day) the option can be exercised |
| **European / American** | European: exercise only at maturity. American: any time up to maturity |
| **Premium** | The price of the option |

A forward contract commits both sides; an option lets the holder walk away if the market price is more favourable.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If the market price beats the strike, a call holder exercises and buys cheaply; if not, the option expires worthless and the holder loses only the premium.

self_check.prompt_text: Who is obliged to act if an option is exercised, the holder or the writer?

items.title: What moves an option's price
items.core_explanation_md:
Five factors, and how a **rise** in each affects the price:

| Factor rises | Call price | Put price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strike price | Falls | Rises |
| Time to maturity | Rises | Rises |
| Stock (underlying) price | Rises | Falls |
| Risk-free interest rate | Rises | Falls |
| Volatility | Rises | Rises |

Why volatility helps both: the holder is protected against bad moves (can walk away) but gains from favourable ones, so more uncertainty adds value to either right. Why time helps both: more time means more chance of a favourable move.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Before maturity an option has **time value** on top of its intrinsic value (the difference between stock and strike, if favourable). Time value shrinks to zero at maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: A stock's volatility doubles. What happens to the call and put prices?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both rise, because greater uncertainty makes either right more valuable.

items.title: Option value bounds and the two pricing models
items.core_explanation_md:
An option never has negative value, and arbitrage fixes a floor:

- **Call**: worth at least the stock price minus the **present value** of the strike, and never less than zero: max[0, S - PV(K)].
- **Put**: worth at least PV(K) - S (or zero).

Two models give the exact price.

- **Binomial model**: price moves at discrete steps, up or down by set percentages with probabilities p and 1 - p; the number of up moves is binomial.
- **Black-Scholes model**: price moves continuously and returns are normal; the call value uses the standard normal cumulative N(d1) and N(d2) with d1 and d2 built from the stock price, strike, rate, volatility and time.

The put follows from put-call parity: P = K e to the minus r(T - t) minus S plus C.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A trader compares the market price with the model value: buy options priced below it, sell those priced above. The details of the formulas are beyond hand calculation; understand the inputs and the direction of each effect.

formula_spec.latex_expression: C \ge \max[0,\ S - PV(K)],\quad P \ge PV(K) - S,\quad C = N(d_1)S - N(d_2)Ke^{-r(T-t)},\quad P = Ke^{-r(T-t)} - S + C

variables.name: Present value of the strike, K discounted at the risk-free rate
Risk-free rate, volatility and time to expiry

assumptions: Black-Scholes: continuously moving prices and normally distributed returns.
The bounds hold for the stated option style and no arbitrage.

Forgetting the floor at zero.
Using N(d2) in place of N(-d2) when writing the put directly (use put-call parity).
